posts.name: Steven Hert
posts.cooked:
I’ve started building ckbup, a small open-source installer and version manager for CKB’s command-line tools, in the spirit of rustup. It’s free and I’m not asking for anything; I’m sharing it early to get feedback from people who actually set up CKB machines.

Why

Getting the CKB tools onto a machine still means a different route for each one:

  • there’s no package-manager install for ckb-cli, only “manually downloading a .zip/.tar.gz from the Releases page” (ckb-cli#685);
  • some tools ship no arm64 builds, so ARM users build from source, which “works but takes 20-30 min” (ckb-light-client#272, fiber#1186);
  • cargo install ckb-cli fails on Windows (ckb-cli#660).

When someone asked in the DevRel AMA about installing tools as one bundle, the answer was that “Bundling them in a separate project should be relatively straightforward” (t/10794/5). ckbup is my attempt at that.

What works today

The first step is merged: ckbup install for ckb-debugger and ckb-cli.

  • It picks the right official release file for your OS and CPU.
  • It checks every download’s SHA-256 against the digest GitHub publishes for the release asset, and against the project’s own checksum file where there is one. A mismatch deletes the download and installs nothing.
  • It installs into ~/.ckbup and tells you how to add it to your PATH.

To try it (needs Rust):

cargo install --git https://github.com/steven3002/ckbup
ckbup install ckb-debugger
ckbup install ckb-cli

Repo: GitHub - steven3002/ckbup: Installer and version manager for CKB tools: ckb, ckb-cli, ckb-debugger, fnn and more. · GitHub

What I found about the releases

Every tool publishes differently:

Tool Latest arm64 builds Windows Checksums
ckb v0.210.0 Linux, macOS x86_64 signature files
ckb-cli v2.0.0 Linux, macOS x86_64 signature files
ckb-debugger v1.1.1 Linux, macOS x86_64 checksum file
fnn v0.9.1 portable builds only x86_64 none
ckb-light-client v0.5.4 none in the stable release x86_64 none
moleculec v0.9.2 no release binaries (crates.io only) none none

No tool ships Windows arm64 builds yet.

Next

  • the other four tools (ckb, fnn, ckb-light-client, moleculec);
  • list, use, update and remove;
  • a source-build fallback where no arm64 binary exists;
  • CI across Linux, macOS and Windows, then a v0.1.0 release.

Feedback welcome

  • Which tools and platforms matter most to you?
  • If you run CKB on ARM boards or in CI, what breaks today?
  • Anything wrong in the table above? I’d like it to be accurate.

posts.name: Steven Hert
posts.cooked:
Update: ckbup now installs five tools.

The second step is merged. ckbup install now covers ckb, fnn and ckb-light-client as well as ckb-debugger and ckb-cli.

cargo install --git https://github.com/steven3002/ckbup
ckbup install ckb
ckbup install fnn
ckbup install ckb-light-client

What changed:

  • The right build for your machine. Each project names its release files differently, and ckbup reads each scheme. For fnn and ckb-light-client it prefers the portable builds: their standard Linux builds need glibc 2.39 and 2.38, while the portable ones run on glibc 2.34. --portable asks for the portable build where a project publishes one. ckb’s release notes recommend it if you see “illegal instruction” errors. CentOS builds are skipped, since upstream plans to stop shipping them.

  • Whole release packages. Config folders and docs stay next to the binary, and companion tools such as fnn-cli go on your PATH too. The copy of ckb-cli bundled inside the ckb release is left off PATH, because ckbup manages ckb-cli as its own tool.

  • Checksums, or a clear stop. Every download is checked against the SHA-256 that GitHub publishes for the release file. Releases published before mid-2025 usually have no checksum at all, so ckbup refuses them unless you pass --allow-unverified:

    $ ckbup install ckb-light-client@v0.4.1
error: GitHub lists no SHA-256 for ckb-light-client_v0.4.1-x86_64-windows.tar.gz, and ckb-light-client
publishes no checksum file for v0.4.1; older releases often have none. Re-run with --allow-unverified
to install it without verification

It also picked up Fiber’s fnn v0.10.1, released this week, as soon as it appeared.

On Windows, ckb-light-client needs the Microsoft Visual C++ runtime; the README says so.

Next: list, use and remove, so you can see what’s installed and switch between versions.

If you run fnn or the light client on an older Linux, I’d like to hear whether the portable builds work for you.

posts.name: Steven Hert
posts.cooked:
Update: ckbup can now list, switch and remove versions.

The third step is merged. You can see what’s installed, switch between versions and remove the ones you don’t need.

cargo install --git https://github.com/steven3002/ckbup
ckbup list                  # every tool, its installed versions and the active one
ckbup list --available      # the newest stable releases, with notes for your machine
ckbup use fnn@v0.9.1        # switch to another installed version
ckbup remove fnn@v0.10.1    # remove one you no longer need

ckbup list on my machine:

ckb               v0.210.0 (active)
ckb-cli           v2.0.0 (active)
ckb-debugger      v1.1.1 (active)
fnn               v0.10.1 (active)
ckb-light-client  v0.5.4 (active)

What changed:

  • list shows all five tools, with installed versions newest first and the active one marked. ckbup list fnn also shows where each version lives.
  • list --available shows the newest 10 stable releases of each tool, and whether your machine has a build and a checksum for each. Releases without a checksum still need --allow-unverified. It uses one GitHub request per tool.
  • use switches versions offline. If the version isn’t installed, it prints the install command instead of downloading anything. fnn’s fnn-cli switches along with fnn.
  • remove won’t delete the version you’re using while other versions are installed; switch with use first. Removing a tool’s last version also takes it off your PATH.
  • Switching works while a tool is running. Windows won’t let a running program be overwritten, so ckbup moves the old files aside instead, and a running program doesn’t block a switch.
  • Installing a second version leaves the current one active, and ckbup tells you how to switch.

Tested on Windows and on Ubuntu 26.04.

Next: update, downloads that resume after a dropped connection, and an optional cache so that switching back to an older version needs no new download.

I haven’t been able to test on macOS yet. If you’re on a Mac, I’d like to hear whether use and remove work for you.

posts.name: Steven Hert
posts.cooked:
Update: ckbup can now update tools, and downloads resume.

The fourth step is merged. ckbup update brings your tools to their latest stable releases, an interrupted download picks up where it stopped, and you can keep downloaded archives so that a reinstall needs no download.

cargo install --git https://github.com/steven3002/ckbup
ckbup update                         # every installed tool, to its latest stable release
ckbup update fnn                     # just one tool
ckbup update --remove-old            # and remove the versions it replaced
ckbup install ckb --keep-archives    # keep the archive for a later reinstall

A version you pick by name stays put until you move it:

$ ckbup install ckb-debugger@v1.1.1
...
ckb-debugger is held at v1.1.1; ckbup update skips it until you run: ckbup update ckb-debugger

$ ckbup update
ckb-debugger v1.1.1 is held; move it to the latest stable release with: ckbup update ckb-debugger

$ ckbup update ckb-debugger
Downloading ckb-debugger_v1.1.2_x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.tar.gz
Verified SHA-256 against GitHub asset digest
Verified SHA-256 against ckb-debugger_v1.1.2_x86_64-pc-windows-msvc-sha256.txt
...
ckb-debugger now follows the latest stable release
ckb-debugger v1.1.1 stays installed. Switch back with: ckbup use ckb-debugger@v1.1.1. Remove it with: ckbup remove ckb-debugger@v1.1.1

What changed:

  • update moves one tool, or every installed tool, to its latest stable release and makes it active. It downloads only when that release isn’t installed yet. The version it replaces stays installed, so switching back is an offline ckbup use; --remove-old removes it instead.

  • Holds. A version you choose by name is held: one you switch to with ckbup use, or one that ckbup install <tool>@<version> makes active. ckbup update skips held tools until you run ckbup update <tool>, and ckbup list marks them. Some ckb and fnn releases need a database migration (ckb v0.106.0 and v0.108.0, fnn v0.8.0), so a node shouldn’t move just because you updated everything else.

  • “Latest stable” means the highest version. GitHub’s own “latest” release goes by date, not version, so it can point at a release candidate that isn’t marked as a pre-release, or at a later fix to an older line. install, update and list --available now all take the highest version that isn’t a draft or a pre-release.

  • Downloads resume. If the connection drops, the next run asks only for the missing bytes:

    Resuming ckb_v0.210.0_x86_64-pc-windows-msvc.zip at 6843056 of 27414343 bytes

    The SHA-256 is still checked on the whole file before anything is installed. Two ckbup runs can’t write the same download at once, and leftovers older than 7 days are cleaned up.

  • Keeping archives is optional. With --keep-archives, or CKBUP_KEEP_ARCHIVES=1 for every command, verified archives stay in ~/.ckbup/cache, and reinstalling a version needs no download. A kept archive is used only after it matches the release’s checksum again. It’s off by default; delete the folder to clear it.

  • Portable builds stay portable. If you installed a portable build, update picks the portable build of the new release too.

  • Executables inside packages now run on Linux. ckb’s bundled ckb-cli used to lose its executable bit when unpacked.

  • Building ckbup now needs Rust 1.89 or newer.

Tested on Windows and on Ubuntu 26.04.

Next: moleculec, and builds from source where a project publishes no binary: ckb-light-client on arm64 and ckb-debugger on Intel Macs. On Windows on Arm, ckbup will use the x64 builds, which Windows runs under emulation.

If your connection often drops mid-download, I’d like to hear whether resuming works for you.
